blocks.x: George William Mitchell is our name.
Just where were you born? In Louisville, Kentucky. What was the date? Oh, 1899. You have the exact birth date? 8th of March. 8th of March, 1899. So you're just about 50... 60.
Oh, you're 60 already?
Oh, that's right, yes. In March. You don't look old at all.
Well, sometimes I feel pretty old.
I do too. Did anyone in your family play music? Your father or any brothers or anyone?
No, there wasn't anybody in my family that I know of that played music. But I can never know of this. None of my family were out. None of my brothers or sisters.
Can you remember the earliest music that you heard?
Oh, well...
That is, around home or was there any bands or parades or anything of that kind that when you were a boy that you can remember?
Well, yes, there were brass bands, you know, as kids usually. I used to follow those brass bands on Sundays. Oh, yeah. In those parades, you know. What kind of bands did they have?
Did they just play marches or did they play sort of jazz?

Well, they just played marches. A straight marches. Yeah. But now there was a band there that used to play Chautauquas and fairs around there. Yeah, they used to play, sometimes play, get in some of those small towns and played dances, you know. But it was a brass band. Yeah. All about, you usually carry about twelve, fifteen pieces. I see.
Were you raised right in the city? Yeah. Of Louisville, right in the city?
Yeah, right in Louisville.
Right in Louisville. Can you tell me how you got interested in wanting to learn to play music yourself?

Well, I was a boy of just about my age, lived next door to me, had a trumpet, and we used to play together, you know, kids together. Yeah. And he used to let me blow on the horn. So that's how I got started on the... Blowing on his horn.
From that.
And his father, had been a clarinet, used to play clarinet in the band. And he taught me the scale, and so I finally got a hold of the cornet.
About how old were you when you started drawing? Well, I was young, very young then, I guess.
I must have been... Oh... I must have been around... Ten, ten, eleven years old. Yeah. Really young.
That was the first instrument you ever had in your hands? Yeah, yeah.

Yeah, yeah. The cornet. The cornet or trumpet? A cornet. The cornet. And I started from that. Then the kid, he and I used to practice together. Eventually I got started over in the church. They had a school band over at the church that I attended. They had a band over there, and went to Catholic school, St. Augustine School. They had a band over there, and one of the fellas that played in there worked for the priest. Yes. Oh, man, he was in the band, and so he had him to show me, help me along with the trumpet.
Did you get into that band then soon?

Well, and, uh, no, I didn't get into the brass band because they had an orchestra there then, was a fellow named Wilbur Winstead, Wilbur Winstead had an orchestra. While then he, uh, he'd taken an interest in me and he put me in his orchestra there, and that way I began to, those different fellas helped me along that way, this is the way I began to learn how to play the trumpet. And then I, uh, he carried me from there, I used to work and reference with him, in his band, and he played in the brass band over in another part of town. Oh, yeah. This band where I was just telling him I used to play the fairs and so on. Oh, yeah. And so he carried me over there to one Sunday, and so they had him bring me back over there, and then I got to play the band, and then all those fellas that just helped me and showed me, you know, helping along. And so that's the way I got started. And there was another fella in there, a very good trumpet player, Robert Williams. He was very good.
Did these boys and fellas all help you to learn music, to read music right away, or did you play by ear at first?
Oh, I started out reading music.
They showed you the scale right away over there. Yes, I started out reading music.

And so that's because I'd go in those bands and I'd play those, they had those orchestrations. Yes. And then afterwards I had playing with piano, just three pieces, piano, trumpet, and drum. Oh, yeah. And we still used the music. We used to get those song sheets in there. Oh, yeah. There was a lot of that sheet music. And we'd play from that and they'd learn how to... You'd transpose. Transpose. And we used to play right off of the... Right off of the... Well, while I think of it, sort of an interruption, one time, a long time ago, somebody told me

you'd been in Louisville and heard some trumpet player by the name of Mitchell and they thought maybe it was your brother. Did you ever have any brothers that played? No. No, no. No, I never had any brothers. So that was a false story then. No, I never had any brothers.
I wondered if it was true. I never had any brothers to play.
What kind of a cornet did you have? Do you remember the make of it when you first started?
No, I don't remember the make of that one, but I do remember where the place I bought it was an old store that sold everything. Just sort of like a junk second hand store.
That's right. Yeah, that's right.
And that cornet was a dollar and a half. Oh, that's cheap. It was a dollar and a half. Good play.
The valves worked all right? Yeah, yeah. And it was one of those... Real short.
Real short. And so my mother, she helped me with... I think I got paid a half a dollar. Down on the street. I don't do a lot of jobs, anyhow. Always done a little...
Lucky to find one for a dollar and a half. Even in those years. That's right.

And so I finally got the... Got the... That cornet and started from that. I kept that cornet for a good while. And so I... Until I got started in playing around with those bands and... And I got doing along pretty well. And so I got started.
Do you remember your first job that you played where you got paid? Or even if you didn't get paid, if it was for some sort of a dance or entertainment or what it was for?

Well, now I can't remember the first job. But I think my first job was with this fellow I was telling you about. Winstead and he paid. I got paid. I can't remember what it was. But... And that's one thing about those fellows. That's where they all... Anytime I would work with this fellow Winstead or... Yeah. Or this other fellow that had the band, the brass band. Why... They'd get... And he paid me the same amount of money that they paid everybody. Always. And so I always had... Little jobs, you know. After they'd take me in the band and every time they'd get a job they'd take... They'd include me. So... If I had a little job during the winter months, why... As soon as summer comes, they'd begin to get... They'd get quite a bit of work in the summer. Yeah. Why then I'd let the job alone and if I couldn't work it in with that and go on with the band. And I... Every summer, I was with the brass band and they played a lot of fairs and that sort of thing. Mostly marches then.
Marches, yeah.
Overtures, I guess.
Yeah, that's right.
That's right.
That's right. But not anything that would be like the jazz... Well, no.

They played a lot of popular... They played a lot of popular numbers, yes. They did, too? But they played a little of everything. I see, yeah. They had some pretty good fellas, pretty good musicians on there. They had... They played these light overtures and those little nice... uh... Uh... Numbers, you know. And marches. And then, uh... They played the popular... I think. Popular tunes. It was... It was... Everything. They played a little everything. But, uh... The fellas... We had fellas in there that played in augustry and they'd get out and, uh... Uh... Uh... We had, uh... We had, uh... Those guys would entertain just like...
I see.

Like an orchestra. The brass band. The brass band. Because there was two groups in there that... That had orchestras, worked orchestras, and they were in that brass band, you know. Yeah, I see. And it wasn't hard for them to... Get together though.
Yeah.

And we had a... Had a guy, uh... A... A... A... Very good entertainer, singer, with the band. Lockwood Lewis. He was... He was... He was very good. And, uh... Everywhere we'd go, we'd... We'd... Pretty... Pretty nice. And so I just... Just went from that and... And I began to like it, you know. I... I... I began to just, uh... Uh... Uh... Uh... Stick with it, you know. And finally, this fellow was... Telling about... William. Bob Williams. He was a... Trumpet player. Man, he was very good. He was a good musician. And he played at, uh... Night clubs. And so... Finally... Uh... The... Those jobs then didn't pay too much... No one got... Money.
Those days.

Yeah. But he... He played there and then whenever they had... Other... Other... Worked dances or... Something like that. They played a lot of dance work in those days. Well then he would leave and go on that because more money. Yeah. And he would put me on the... Take his place in the cabaret that night. And so that way I got... Got a little experience of playing, uh... Uh... Offering for entertainers. Sure. And so from that way I... I... I got into playing... Playing... Cabaret... And... Playing for entertainers. Yeah. And played in the... I played for... Several years in the theater... What was the... Waterville House where the pictures of Waterville... Oh yes.
Right in Louisville.
Right in Louisville.
Yeah. Remember the name of that theater?
Now... Let's see... They changed the name of that theater... Several... And I think it was... What? It was Dream Man Theater... I don't know... Next...
It's been so long...
I know they changed names a lot of times that way... Yeah... Uh...
I think it was the Lyric... I just can't remember now...
But... They changed the name... How long did you stay in Louisville then... And... Doing that kind of work... And when did you leave town there? Well... After... After a few years...
I guess I was around... About... 16 or 17... I... I... Went out on the...

And... I... I... Went out on the... And... I... I... I... I... I... I... I... I... I... Went out on... A friend of mine was a drummer... He'd been... Went out on the road with those... Ministral bands... Oh yes... And so he... Taught me into going with the... Ministral bands... So I went with the... Ministral bands there...
That was back in...
That must have been back in... 17... 16... 17... Remember whose show it was? Uh... One... I was with two of them... I think it was... They called... One... Rabbit's Foot... Oh yeah...
The Rabbit's Foot... That went down south... Yeah... That's right... That's right...
Down near New Orleans... That's right... I left... Left Louisville and went to... Join them in... Mississippi...
I believe...
Yeah... That's where they... Worked down in there... And then... What was the name of this other one? A.G. Allen... I believe it was...
Not A.G. Allen... I don't know... A.G. Fields... Was that the big... No... Was Al...
What was...
Well that's alright... Don't worry... No... It wasn't Allen... What was the name of that...
Well I know... Rabbit's Foot was one...
Yeah... There must have been a lot of those...
Yeah... And then there was... This fellow that had the band there... It was Mark... He was from St. Louis... Clanness... He had a good band too...
Is there any fellows from New Orleans in the band that you can remember? In the Rabbit's Foot...

I can't remember any fellows from New Orleans... Let's see... No... I can't remember any of the boys from New Orleans... There was... No... No... No I can't... But there was a very good trumpet player there... But there was a very good trumpet player there... But I was always... Tip된 stuff... Tip된 stuff... Tip된 stuff... Tip된 stuff... Tip된 stuff... Well, I came back and worked around with the dance bands around there. And then I left, left Louisville
from Chicago here. That's the best part. Came here in about 1920? About 1920. Yeah, that's

Well, I started, I came here, the job I came here after, I don't know what happened. The fella, what did happen after this. Something happened that I couldn't go on that job on account of some union. Yes. Yeah. I understand. And so I stayed around here and I went, worked with the, with the, uh, uh, the Vaudeville act, uh, show, this, uh, Miller, what is his name, uh, uh, uh, they were playing down at the, uh, this theater on, uh, the 31st, uh, uh, they just toured that theater. Oh, the, the Graham. The Graham Theater, yes. Yeah. And I, I worked in there for, for a while until I got, then, uh, uh, eventually got started playing dances around here. And then, I, I got on a job with, uh, John Wycliffe. Oh, yeah. I've heard of this man. See, he was from Louisville, too. See, I knew him. Oh, he was from Louisville. Yeah. I knew him. So, he, uh, he gave me a job. Well, he, then, uh, I had a chance to work with him at the, uh, at the, uh, old entertainers. Yeah. He wanted me to work with him. This same fellow, I was telling you about, Williams, Bobby Williams from Louisville. Oh, yeah. Well, he was working with him at that time. They had a, they had a band that played, uh, all types of.
I forget, where were the entertainers on State Street, or? Uh, uh, entertainers on 35th,

between, uh, uh, near Indiana. Oh, yeah. On 35th. Yeah, sure. Yeah. On 35th near Indiana. Yeah. On the south side of the street. That's right. Yeah. That's right. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. And, uh, that, that was, that was a, a good spot around there. Then, uh, that's when Joe was, was, uh, was in, was going big, too, around there, around at that time. Joe Oliver? Joe Oliver, yeah. Joe Oliver, yeah. Was he at the Royal Garden? He was at the Royal Garden? No, wait a minute. No, wait a minute. Now, I think he was at the, I think he was at the Dreamland, early part of the night. Where were we at? And he was down on 27th and, and State. Oh, yeah, the Pekin. Pekin. Yeah. Pekin, yeah. That's where he was. Uh-huh. Okay. Down in the Pekin. And, uh, I think after that he worked at the, uh, at the Royal Garden. Royal Garden? Yeah. But that, that, that, that guy, he was, uh, my favorite trumpet player.
Really was. In jazz playing. Did their band sound much different than the music in Louisville?

That it's different type, or? Well, yes. South the same? Yes, uh, the New Orleans band, and, we, I, I, I, I, because when I, I came to Chicago and heard Joe and those boys from New Orleans, why, I, I, I just, I never heard nothing like that. Them guys out, I, I, I. Really liked it. Yeah. Uh-huh. Yeah. Uh, I, I, I think it was, it was different. Because one thing, I think, uh, Borgon, really, uh, it didn't, wasn't, it was, uh, I don't know, didn't have the, the style. The style was different, you know? Was there a difference in playing the melody, or a difference in the rhythm and the beat, or what? Yeah, I, I, I, I think it was in the, in the melody, and the melody, and, uh, well, I guess, rhythm, too. Because these boys had a rhythm, different rhythm. Do you remember any of the other trumpet players from New Orleans, like Freddie Keppard? Freddie Keppard? Well, yes. Oh, sure you would have known him later, anyway. Was he here when you came up? Yeah, Freddie Keppard was here, yeah, he, and, uh, there was another boy from, uh, New Orleans, uh, uh, oh, awesome. He, uh, he, uh, he joined, uh, went to, left, went to New York with, uh, Fletcher Henderson. Uh, Tommy Ladner? Tommy Ladner. Oh, yeah. Yeah, Tommy Ladner. He was good, I, I, I thought he was, he was a good guy. Oh, yeah. I knew him in New York. You did, yeah. Nice fella. Yeah, yes, uh-huh, I thought he was, he was a good, good drunk. Well, I, I, I like the style, but I don't know, I like Joe, I like Joe's style.
How did Joe and, when the, when Louis Armstrong came up to join him, how did they compare? Was Joe was powerful, or more powerful, and Louis, or how?

Well, I never, I never heard Joe in person. Yeah, well, Joe was, uh, they, uh, Louis could get over his, his, his, his trumpet, and, and, uh, I don't know the, the, the playing, that playing was, was, uh, I don't know the, the, I don't know how to explain it, but it was a little different, but they were both good, but Louis was, was, uh, Louis was, was, uh, he could get over his trumpet, and, uh, fast fingering and all. Yeah, yes, uh-huh. And, uh, but Joe had a lot of, a lot of, uh, a lot of odd, sort of, uh, melodies and things he could, he could get into, work into. Was he powerful, and a big tone, or, uh? Well, no, I think, I think Louis had the best tone.
Uh-huh. I think it was. Did Joe use a lot of mutes, or derby, or what did he use?

A lot, that, that, that, that's where he was famous for, using a mute, he had one of those old, mutes, old, short, old, kind of, you remember? A little con mute, I've seen that, like light bulbs. That's right, yeah. Well, that guy could use that and use his hand over that and make, make that, that corner talk.
Did you ever see Joe, did he use the rubber plunger?

No, no, he never used the, I, I think that's what started most of the other fellas using the plungers from Joe, the way he, he could use his hand over that, that mute, he could, and there was, uh, I don't know what it was, a tune that he could, he played and it was almost, it sounded like somebody talking. Oh, yeah. Yeah, the guy, he, I don't know, he was, he was very good with that, I never heard anybody work with a mute.
Did he ever use a derby hand?
Well, yes, he, used derby too. But, uh, not with the mute. Yeah, not the long. Yeah, usually he'd use the open horn with the derby.
But he'd hold that in his hand, the derby in his hand.
Yeah, the derby, yeah, that's right. Hold the derby in his hand.
Because sometimes now they have them on a stand, you know, they just blow down into it.
Yeah, yeah, that's right.
But he'd use the hand.

Yeah, use the hand. The derby. That's right, yeah. He was, uh, he was very good. I, I, uh, I don't know, Joe, Joe was my favorite. Although Lewis, Lewis could, he had a, a style that was, it was good, very good. And he was, but it was different from, from Joe's, uh, they were two different. Different types. Yeah, types. But, uh, they worked well together. I never heard of two trumpets team together as well as one of them. Joe, he, he used to have a way of playing and, uh, right in the middle, of course, they'd take a break. Yeah. Out of two bars there. And, uh, whatever he would make, he would, they would play it through down to the, uh, first ending of the, of the tune. And Joe would make his, whatever he was gonna make in that next break. He'd make it down in that first, first ending. By himself. He'd repeat, yeah. Do it. Then Lewis, Lewis, Lewis, Lewis know what's coming. Do it soft, just so? No, no, he'd make it play it in there. Play it, play it in there, part of the ending. That's right. Play it in there and he'd make something, he'd rattle it off, you know, less, uh, yeah. Then when you get back to that, that, uh, go down there again, Yeah, Louis know what's coming up. It'd make a break and the two trumpets are taken. Yeah. Yeah, that's, that's, that's.

They made some of those on some records, I've heard that. Uh-huh. I never noticed if he did it in the ending. I'll have to listen to those records again and see if he does something on the ending. Yeah, well that was Joe, that was, Joe, he would, yeah.

He, well I tell you, I don't think he, I've never heard, I've never heard, heard many recordings of Joe and what recordings that he made. I didn't, didn't, uh, I don't think it, it, it gives him, you know.
It doesn't justice. No.
That's what I've heard. No. People tell me that too. No, it, it doesn't because, uh, uh, I don't think he made many, Joe didn't make many.
No, they were so early too. Yes, that's right.

That's right. That's right. That's right. That's right. That's right. It didn't sound anything like Joe. Uh, because I remember at the time that they, those records come out, you know. But, uh, I don't, don't think it'd give Joe justice. Yeah. Because he, that guy was, he was very, very good at, uh, the style that he, he played in. Yeah.
Did you ever play with him?

Well, I'd sit in, I'd sit in with him, go down to the Dreamland there. And, uh, I could never, never do much, but, like, of course I wasn't, uh, couldn't, uh, have them grab those ideas, you know. Yeah, it's hard to learn right away. Yeah, uh-huh. Something new. Yeah, uh-huh. But, uh, I have, I've played, played in, and here, here, when I, I went to play in Milwaukee for, oh, for about a year, left Chicago, and went up there for a year, a couple years. And that's before he enlarged his band, he, and he, yeah, he, he didn't know where I was. He, he said he would have, uh, would have, uh, when he enlarged his band, he was gonna put me in there. Yeah, at the plantation, that big band. Uh, uh, no, that's before Lewis come. Oh, before that. Before Lewis come, yeah. But, uh-huh. But, uh-huh. But he, uh, uh, he didn't know where I was. What was that? I, uh, I, uh, worked with, uh, used to work with, uh, uh, uh, Sunset, this other. Dickerson? Dickerson. Carol? Carol Dickerson. I worked there. Carol Dickerson.
I knew you said. Who else was in the band then?

segments.title: Birth in Louisville, 1899
segments.summary: Mitchell gives his name, birthplace Louisville and birth date, 8 March 1899.

segments.title: No musicians in the family; brass bands and parades
segments.summary: No one in his family played. He followed marching brass bands on Sundays; one band played fairs and Chautauquas.

segments.title: Getting a cornet from a neighbor boy at ten or eleven
segments.summary: A neighbor boy let him blow his trumpet, the boy's father taught him the scale, and he got a cornet at about ten or eleven.

segments.title: Winstead's orchestra, the brass band and learning to read
segments.summary: Wilbur Winstead took him into his orchestra and then the brass band; he learned from orchestrations and sheet music and says he had no trumpet-playing brother.

segments.title: The first cornet, bought for a dollar and a half
segments.summary: He recalls buying a short second-hand cornet for $1.50 in a junk store and keeping it a good while.

segments.title: First paid jobs and summers with the brass band
segments.summary: Winstead and the brass band paid him the same as everyone; summers were fairs, with marches, overtures and popular tunes.

segments.title: Bob Williams, cabaret work and Louisville theater
segments.summary: Singer Lockwood Lewis and trumpeter Bob Williams are recalled; Williams let him sub in the cabaret, leading to years playing a Louisville theater whose name he cannot recall.

segments.title: Leaving Louisville for the Rabbit's Foot and other minstrel shows
segments.summary: At 16 or 17 a drummer friend got him onto minstrel shows, including the Rabbit's Foot in Mississippi; he cannot pin down the other show.

segments.title: New Orleans players in the shows, trumpeter Mason, back to Louisville
segments.summary: Asked about New Orleans men in the Rabbit's Foot, he recalls none but praises trumpeter Mason, stays about a year, then returns to Louisville dance bands.

segments.title: Arriving in Chicago about 1920, the Graham Theater and John Wycliffe
segments.summary: He comes to Chicago around 1920, is blocked from a job by the union, plays vaudeville at the Graham Theater, then joins John Wycliffe's band with Bobby Williams at the Entertainers.

segments.title: Joe Oliver on the South Side and the New Orleans style
segments.summary: He places Oliver at the Pekin, Dreamland and Royal Garden, says the New Orleans players sounded unlike Louisville bands, and mentions Keppard and Tommy Ladnier.

segments.title: Comparing Joe Oliver and Louis Armstrong
segments.summary: Mitchell says Armstrong had the better tone and fast fingering while Oliver had odd melodic ideas, though both were good.

segments.title: Oliver's mute work, derby and two-trumpet breaks
segments.summary: He describes Oliver's talking mute and hand derby, and how Oliver and Armstrong played their breaks together.

segments.title: Oliver's recordings, and sitting in at Dreamland
segments.summary: He thinks Oliver's few records do not do him justice and says he sat in with him at the Dreamland.

segments.title: Milwaukee with Doc Holley, and Carroll Dickerson
segments.summary: Before Armstrong joined Oliver he spent a year or two in Milwaukee with Doc Holley's band at Lewis Castle Ice Garden, then came back to work with Carroll Dickerson.

segments.title: Dickerson's band personnel and Lil Armstrong's band at Dreamland
segments.summary: He lists Dickerson sidemen (Henry Gordon, Buster Bailey, Rudy Jackson, drummers) and says he worked with Lil Armstrong at Dreamland; he struggles to recall the others.

segments.title: Dreamland years: Ollie Powers, Jimmie Noone and Charlie Cook
segments.summary: Around 1926-27 he worked with Ollie Powers, Jimmie Noone and Charlie Cook at Dreamland and White City.

segments.title: Freddie Keppard, Oliver and Armstrong compared
segments.summary: He swaps places with Keppard in Cook's band and judges Keppard strong but below Armstrong and Oliver; Armstrong had better technique, Oliver better ideas.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: How he came to record with Jelly Roll Morton
segments.summary: Mitchell was called in when Morton's planned men fell through; Allen relays that Morton rated him above Armstrong and Simeon as clarinet favorite.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Rehearsals with Morton and how he guided the band
segments.summary: Morton wrote out parts, played or hummed ideas, and wanted sidemen to add their own; Mitchell says he needed a written guide.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Where the Morton sessions were rehearsed and recorded
segments.summary: He made many records he later forgot; rehearsals were at the union hall or places the publisher arranged, and one recording was in a hotel.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Only one trumpet and one clarinet on the Morton records
segments.summary: Mitchell is sure he was the only trumpet and Simeon the only clarinet, rejecting rumors of Lee Collins or extra clarinets.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Buying a Harry B. Jay cornet after Muggsy lent his
segments.summary: The cornet he used for the Morton records was a Chicago-made Jay, bought after Muggsy Spanier left his horn at a 35th Street club.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Muggsy, Darnell Howard, Pops Foster and old Chicago bassists
segments.summary: Chat about where Muggsy, Darnell Howard and Pops Foster are now, and about bassists Eddie Garland and Bill Johnson.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: The Lil Armstrong recording date
segments.summary: Allen asks about the Columbia sides with Lil Armstrong, Ory, St. Cyr and Johnny Dodds; Mitchell barely remembers the single date.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Records with Jimmy O'Brien, a singer and possibly Ida Cox
segments.summary: He vaguely recalls recording with a clarinetist named O'Brien and with blues singers, but cannot identify them.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Rehearsals and retakes on the Morton dates
segments.summary: They rehearsed two or three times and sometimes had to remake a number.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Sidemen: Bud Scott, Johnny Lindsey and Roy Palmer
segments.summary: He worked with banjoist and guitarist Bud Scott, Johnny Lindsey and trombonist Roy Palmer on other jobs, though he cannot place Scott on the Morton dates.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Drummer Andrew Hilaire
segments.summary: Mitchell remembers Hilaire as a good, reading drummer from Louisiana who has since died.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: How Morton stomped off tunes, set dynamics and arranged solos
segments.summary: Morton gave the tempo, shaped the phrasing, let players go their own way on solos, and the order of choruses was set beforehand.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Morton as a person, and recordings as the only work with him
segments.summary: Mitchell says he always got along with Morton, who liked to kid, but never worked a job with him, only recordings.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Someday Sweetheart, bass clarinet and violin
segments.summary: Allen asks about extra instruments on Someday Sweetheart; Mitchell remembers only Simeon on clarinet.

segments.chapter: Jelly Roll Morton and other records
segments.title: Using the mute: Oliver's effect he could not match
segments.summary: On the Morton records he played open horn; he never mastered mute work like Oliver, who remained his favorite.

segments.title: Sticking to the melody, limited range and mouthpiece
segments.summary: He explains his melodic style, small range, high notes and a medium mouthpiece, and his poor early foundation on trumpet.

segments.title: No lessons, instruction books and range problems
segments.summary: He never took lessons, learned from other musicians and instruction books, and blames not making a living from music for his unreliable upper range.

segments.title: Playing with Earl Hines at the Grand Terrace
segments.summary: Mitchell played several years in Hines's band at the Grand Terrace, alongside Shirley Clay, but did not record with him.

segments.title: Other records: Johnny Dodds, Nat Dominique, O'Brien, Blythe, Ma Rainey
segments.summary: Asked about other recordings, he recalls Dodds on a Lil date, working with Dominique, and a date with Jimmy O'Brien that may have been Blythe's with Ma Rainey.

segments.title: Last regular bands: Dickerson, Cook, Hines, WPA band and Zilner Randolph
segments.summary: After Hines the Depression cut work; he played in Norman Black's WPA brass band and finally Zilner Randolph's dance band.

segments.title: Helping a kids' brass band in Louisville
segments.summary: He rehearsed a girls' welfare worker's children's brass band in Louisville and later met former pupils.

segments.title: Advice to young players: learn the instrument, learn to read
segments.summary: He advises learning to handle the instrument and to read, discusses reading versus improvising on the Morton dates, and dislikes bop's complexity.

segments.title: Anything to add; never wrote music
segments.summary: Asked for a favorite piece or compositions, he says he never wrote any.

segments.title: When he switched to trumpet; cornet on the records
segments.summary: He thinks he got a trumpet before Chicago but used his Jay cornet through the Hines years, always open horn.

segments.title: How he practiced while working nights
segments.summary: He practiced long notes and exercises but could not do much while working nights.

segments.title: Printed Melrose arrangements and the Victor reissue
segments.summary: They played printed orchestrations on the Morton dates and added parts; Allen tells him about the Victor reissue of the sides.

segments.title: Closing praise, self-assessment and goodbye
segments.summary: Allen thanks him and praises his drive; Mitchell says he never satisfied himself, and the tape ends with a photograph request.

segments.title: Radio sermon recorded over the tape end
segments.summary: A Prayer Tower Church of God in Christ radio sermon on Pilate and Jesus, closed by an announcer, unrelated to the interview.
